opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that foundation models have given robotics a lot on the "knowing" side and much less on the "doing" side. If you take a large language model or a vision-language model, it already has a surprising amount of common sense about the world. It knows that a cup goes on a table and not on the ceiling, that you open a fridge before you take something out, roughly what a kitchen looks like. For high-level planning, breaking "clean up the room" into steps, recognizing objects, following instructions, that transfers pretty well. That used to be a hard part of robotics, and now it's mostly something you can get off the shelf.

The gap is the physical, low-level part: contact, force, timing, how things deform, how much friction there is when you grab a towel versus a glass. None of that is really in internet text or even in internet video in a form a model can learn to act from. Video shows you what happened, but not the torques and the feedback loop that made it happen. So robots still have to learn the sensorimotor layer mostly from their own experience, and that data is expensive. You can't scrape it. You have to collect it with real hardware or with simulation, and simulation has its own fidelity problems.

From my side, coming from systems and architectures, there's also a gap in how these models run. Robots need to react in tens of milliseconds, often on a power budget, often on the device. They also need to process long streams of sensor data: video, proprioception, maybe audio, over minutes or hours of a task. That's exactly where standard transformers struggle, because attention gets expensive as context grows and latency matters. So I think a lot of the progress will come from more efficient architectures, things like state space models or hybrids, and better inference, so that a model can keep a long memory of what it's seen and still respond in real time.

So the summary is that foundation models give you a strong prior about the world and about language. What robots still need to learn is the embodied part: fine-grained control, physics, recovering from mistakes. And they need to do it within real-time and compute constraints that the current generation of models wasn't designed for. Closing that gap is partly a data problem and partly an efficiency problem, and I think both are very solvable over the next few years.

r001.rationale: It says language and vision-language models can handle high-level planning, including breaking a task into steps.

r002.rationale: It explains that internet text and video lack the physical interaction data—such as forces, torques, and feedback—needed for models to learn sensorimotor actions.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd frame it is that foundation models have gotten really good at the parts of intelligence that we have a lot of data for, which is basically everything that lives on the internet. Language, images, video, code. If you think about what a robot needs, a surprising amount of that transfers. The high-level stuff, like understanding a scene, parsing an instruction, planning a sequence of steps, knowing that a cup is for holding liquid and that you shouldn't tip it, that's all stuff these models already have a decent prior on. So that gap has actually closed a lot faster than people expected a few years ago.

Where the gap is still really wide is the low-level stuff. The actual control, the contact-rich manipulation, the physics. There's just no internet-scale dataset of torque commands and tactile feedback. The data we have is tiny by comparison, it's expensive to collect, it's heterogeneous across different robot bodies, and it's often noisy. So the models that come out of pretraining don't really know what it feels like to grasp something, or how a deformable object behaves, or how to recover when a grasp slips. That's the piece robots still have to learn, and they have to learn it largely from their own experience or from teleoperation data.

The other thing I'd point to is the systems side, which is where I spend a lot of my time. A language model can take a second to respond and nobody cares. A robot can't. You need the policy running at tens or hundreds of hertz, often on hardware that's power constrained, with latency that's actually bounded. A lot of the architectures that work great in the cloud were not designed with that in mind. So part of the gap is modeling, part of it is data, but a real part of it is just making inference fast and predictable enough that the model can live in a control loop. I think that constraint is going to shape what architectures win in robotics, and it's not obvious it'll be the same ones that won in language.

r001.rationale: The response says foundation models have a useful prior for robotics tasks including “planning a sequence of steps,” which communicates that they can provide high-level plans.

r002.rationale: It explains there is no internet-scale data for torque commands and tactile feedback, and that this leaves pretrained models without experience grasping or responding to slips.

astra-6.text:
I think foundation models give you a really useful prior about the world. They can recognize objects, understand instructions, and maybe break a task into steps. But there’s still a gap between knowing what you want to do and knowing how to execute it physically.

If you ask a robot to pick up a cup, identifying the cup is only part of the problem. How should it grasp it? How much force should it apply? What should it do if the cup starts slipping? Those decisions depend on feedback from the environment, and they have to happen quickly.

So I think the question is how much you can transfer from models trained on text and images, and how much has to come from interaction. My intuition is that you can transfer quite a lot of the high-level understanding, but you still need robot data to learn the connection between actions and their consequences. And collecting that data is much harder than collecting text from the internet.

The exciting part is figuring out how to use that prior so the robot doesn’t have to learn everything from scratch—while still allowing it to learn from what actually happens when it acts.

r001.rationale: The response says foundation models can understand instructions and break a task into steps, communicating their ability to provide high-level plans for a robot.

r002.rationale: It says robots need data to learn how actions affect outcomes and that collecting robot interaction data is harder than collecting internet text, identifying a data gap behind the physical interaction limitation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think foundation models give robots a useful starting point. They can recognize objects, understand instructions, and bring in a lot of knowledge about the world. But there’s still a gap between knowing what a task means and knowing how to execute it physically.

If I ask a robot to pick up a cup, recognizing the cup is only part of the problem. It has to figure out how to grasp it, respond when it slips, and adjust to things it can’t see, like its weight or how much friction there is. That requires learning from interaction and closing the loop between perception and action.

So I think a big question is how to connect the broad knowledge in these models with the experience a robot gets in its environment. And how do we make that learning efficient? You want the robot to generalize to a new object or a new room without having to collect a huge amount of data for every situation.

r001.rationale: The response mentions recognizing instructions and world knowledge, but does not say that existing language models can provide high-level plans for robots.

r002.rationale: The response says robots need to learn through interaction and that gathering large amounts of data is undesirable, but it does not identify a lack of physical-action data as the reason existing models lack needed interaction capabilities.
